newsitem.title: JAPAN: U.S. pledges $400 million to ADB.
newsitem.headline: U.S. pledges $400 million to ADB.

text.p: The United States agreed to give $400 million in loans to Asia's poorest nations, despite worries of a pullback of American aid under a Republican Congress, the Asian Development Bank (ADB) said on Friday.
"My message to American Congressmen is that we very much want them to approve, to support this contribution," ADB president Mitsuo Sato told a news conference.
U.S. pledges need congressional approval before they can be paid.
Some U.S. legislators have balked at paying millions more dollars to multinational agencies on the grounds that the United States cannot afford to be as generous as it has been in the past.
Sato said the United States was "a kind of Asian-Pacific nation" and added that strengthening its support to the ADB was of mutual benefit to the United States and Asia.

The agreement was reached after two days of negotiations in Tokyo by ADB donors over replenishing the Asian Development Fund (ADF), an interest-free loan facility aimed at improving the living conditions of Asia's 750 million poor people.
The seventh replenishment covers a four-year period to 2000.
"The significance of this is that it means we can maintain ADF as a single fund with full burden sharing and participation by the United States during the entire replenishment period," Sato said.
But the U.S. contribution was less than the pledge it made at the previous agreement, which was $680 million.
The United States had yet to fully honour that pledge, with $237 million still in arrears, but it had promised to pay it off in the next four years, Sato said.

Donor nations such as U.S. and European nations have been reluctant to commit new funding because of domestic budgetary constraints and because they feel that the newly wealthy Asian states should be shouldering more of the burden.
Sato said that Euorpe has maintained its strong commitment to the fund though their contribution had declined slightly from the previous round.

Many donors gave conditions to the replenishment, such as a review by the bank of the "graduation" of borrower nations to lenders, a toughening of repayment conditions and a larger contribution to the fund by the bank itself.
ADF loans, provided to the poorest of the ADB's developing member countries, are interest free, have repayment periods of 30 years or more and carry a service charge of one percent annually.
Asian donors did heed the call and increased their share of the burden to half of the total replenishment in the current round.

First-time contributors Malaysia and Thailand intend to provide $10 million and $4 million respectively, while South Korea, also a graduate from borrower to lender, raised its contribution from $15 million to $54.3 million.
Singapore opted out from the seventh replenishment, but Sato said the ADB would continue to have talks with the island state on what it can do for the bank.
Japan remains the largest contributor at $1.02 billion.
Indonesia and Philippines were also up for consideration to graduate from borrower to lender status, Sato said.
